title: Hundreds of streaming services and nothing to watch
gist: A Gracenote (Nielsen) survey of 3,000 streaming users across six countries finds content discovery, not content scarcity, is the core pain point: over half say abundance makes choosing harder, 47% spend more time searching than a year ago, and 72.3% want a consolidated cross-service guide. Frustration is pushing some viewers toward free ad-supported services.

themes.theme: Discovery, not content, is the bottleneck

insights.claim: Gracenote's 2026 survey of 3,000 adult streaming users in the US, Brazil, France, Germany, Mexico and the UK found over 51 percent say the abundance of content and services makes it harder to find something to watch.
insights.speaker: Scharon Harding
insights.so_what: Fragmentation is eroding user experience, a churn and engagement risk for streamers.

insights.claim: 19.2 percent of streaming users always or often can't decide what to watch and abandon streaming for something else, and 27.4 percent always or often fail to find a specific program they wanted.
insights.speaker: Scharon Harding
insights.so_what: Quantifies lost viewing sessions, directly hitting engagement and ad inventory.

insights.claim: 47 percent of respondents spend more time looking for something to watch than a year ago, averaging 12 minutes per search.
insights.speaker: Scharon Harding
insights.so_what: Worsening discovery trend creates opening for aggregation and UX vendors.

insights.claim: Gracenote argues that despite large catalogs and personalization data, audiences are not finding what they want and content discovery challenges are mounting, framing UX as the future of streaming.
insights.speaker: Scharon Harding
insights.so_what: Competitive advantage in streaming may shift from content spend to discovery UX.
insights.quote: Audiences, however, aren’t finding what they’re looking for, and content discovery challenges are mounting,

insights.claim: 31 percent of respondents have yet to find a good source of recommendations for their personal tastes, despite Netflix and Amazon Prime Video using AI search and Tubi using user-generated playlists.
insights.speaker: Scharon Harding
insights.so_what: Existing AI recommendation investments have not solved discovery, leaving room for differentiation.

insights.claim: Nearly 52 percent of streaming users frequently don't know which channel or service a specific sports event is on, even as streamers pay large sums for live sports to grow ad businesses.
insights.speaker: Scharon Harding
insights.so_what: Undermines ROI on expensive sports rights if viewers can't find the events.
insights.quote: “Sports events that are behind subscription paywalls are often hidden from traditional search, which inhibits discovery,”

insights.claim: Almost 35 percent of respondents spend more time on free ad-supported streaming services like Tubi or The Roku Channel because subscription services such as Netflix and Disney+ have become overwhelming.
insights.speaker: Scharon Harding
insights.so_what: Tailwind for FAST platforms' viewing share and ad revenue at the expense of SVOD.

insights.claim: 72.3 percent of streaming users want a consolidated guide to programming across all the streaming services they use, signaling demand for a return of TV-Guide-style listings.
insights.speaker: Scharon Harding
insights.so_what: Opportunity for aggregators, TV OS makers and metadata providers to own the cross-service guide layer.

insights.claim: Research firm Parks and Associates counts hundreds of streaming services in the market this month.
insights.speaker: Scharon Harding
